### Introduction

Netflix has been publishing "What We Watched" reports every 6 months since 2023. The data contains the number of hours watched for each title. This data is very useful to get insights and draw conclusions from the information of the past 3 years. This data was released to help advertisers get a sense of the number of people who would see their ads, and help creators get a sense of viewership in order to check they were getting paid accordingly.

In this report I analyzed the 7 reports that are available which contain data between 2023H1 all the way to 2026H1, and gathered information regarding what types of content are watched the most (in hours). I cleaned the data and created tables in order to have a visual on the data and also provided a strategy memo you can find at the bottom. 

### Data Acquisition and Cleaning

```{r}
#' Acquire Netflix What We Watched Reports
#' 
#' This function will acquire and standardize all data for MP#01
#' from Netflix. Because Netflix hosts the data files behind a CDN, we
#' are accessing the release pages and automatically extracting links to the
#' relevant files (with CDN hash). 
#' 
#' After import, files are stacked vertically and some basic cleaning is
#' performed. 
load_netflix_data <- function(){
  # Note to students: Make sure you have installed the tidyverse and fs packages
  #                   before beginning this assignment. If you aren't sure,
  #                   simply run `library(tidyverse)` at your R Console and, if
  #                   you don't see an error message, `tidyverse` has been 
  #                   installed. (Same for `fs`) If you still need to install
  #                   either package, use the `install.packages` function as 
  #                   demonstrated in class.
  library(tidyverse)
  library(rvest)
  library(readxl)
  library(fs)
  
  data_dir <- path("data", "mp01")
    
  if(!dir_exists(data_dir)){
    dir_create(data_dir, showWarnings=FALSE, recurse=TRUE)
  }
  
  NETFLIX_URLS <- list(
    `2023H1` = "https://about.netflix.com/news/what-we-watched-a-netflix-engagement-report",
    `2023H2` = "https://about.netflix.com/news/what-we-watched-the-second-half-of-2023",
    `2024H1` = "https://about.netflix.com/news/what-we-watched-the-first-half-of-2024",
    `2024H2` = "https://about.netflix.com/news/what-we-watched-the-second-half-of-2024",
    `2025H1` = "https://about.netflix.com/news/what-we-watched-the-first-half-of-2025",
    `2025H2` = "https://about.netflix.com/news/what-we-watched-the-second-half-of-2025",
    `2026H1` = "https://about.netflix.com/news/what-we-watched-the-first-half-of-2026"
  )
  
  download_if_needed <- function(url, local){
    if(!file_exists(local)){
      download.file(url, local, quiet = TRUE, mode = "wb")
    }
    
    return(local)
  }
    
  NETFLIX_URLS |> 
    map(read_html) |> 
    map(html_element, xpath = "//a[contains(@href, '.xlsx')]") |> 
    map_chr(html_attr, "href") |> 
    enframe("period", "url") |> 
   mutate(path = path(data_dir, paste0(period, ".xlsx")), 
          path = map2(url, path, download_if_needed), 
          data = map(path, read_excel, skip=3, na="*"), 
          data = map(data, \(x) x |> mutate(`Release Date` = as.Date(`Release Date`)))) |>
    unnest(data) |> 
    select(-url, -path) |> 
    mutate(year=str_sub(period, 1, 4), 
           half=str_sub(period, start=6), 
           period_start = make_date(year, if_else(half==1, 1, 7), 1), 
           period_end = make_date(year, if_else(half==1, 7, 12), if_else(half==1, 30, 31))) |> 
    filter(!is.na(`Hours Viewed`)) |> 
    mutate(live_event = !is.na(Runtime) & str_detect(Runtime, "\\d+:\\d+\\*"), 
           clean_time = str_remove(Runtime, fixed("*")),
           Runtime = 60 * hour(hm(clean_time)) + minute(hm(clean_time))) |>
    select(-clean_time) |>
    mutate(Runtime = coalesce(Runtime, mean(Runtime, na.rm=TRUE)), 
           .by=Title, 
           Title = stringi::stri_trans_general(Title, "Latin-ASCII"),
           Title = str_remove(Title, " // .*"), 
           Title = str_remove(Title, "[^[:ascii:]].*"), 
           Title = str_trim(Title)) |>
    filter_out(Title == "") |>
    select(year,
           period,
           period_start,
           period_end,
           Title,
           -half,
           Runtime,
           Views,
           `Hours Viewed`,
           `Release Date`,
           `Available Globally?`,
           live_event) |>
    rename(title = Title,
           runtime = Runtime,
           views = Views,
           hours_viewed = `Hours Viewed`,
           release_date = `Release Date`,
           available_globally = `Available Globally?`) |>
    mutate(
      year = as.integer(year),
      available_globally = available_globally == "Yes"
    )
}

NETFLIX_DATA <- load_netflix_data()
```

### Initial Data Exploration

```{r}
library(skimr)
glimpse(NETFLIX_DATA)
```

```{r}
skim(NETFLIX_DATA)
```



After reviewing the data summary, we see we have 11 columns, 61,892 rows that contains a title viewership in a 6 month period, and the columns have the correct type now that we cleaned them. We can also see that we can rely more on the `year` and `hours_viewed` because there are no missing cells there, versus `runtime` (around 21% missing) and `views` (almost 30% missing), where we have some data missing. We can also see that we can rely on the data from `period_start` and `period_end` since there are also no missing values there compared to `release_date` where we have 35,251 missing cells and only 43% complete. Also, both `available_globally` and `live_event` are pretty reliable since only 2 rows are missing in `available_globally`. Having clarity on the above will help us make sure we are relying on complete data to make our analysis more accurate.

### Exploratory questions

```{r}
library(scales)
```

###### 1. What date range is covered by this data set?

```{r}
#Date range
first_date <- min(NETFLIX_DATA$period_start)
last_date  <- max(NETFLIX_DATA$period_end)

```

The date range goes from `r first_date` until `r last_date`.

###### 2. How many different shows and movies are covered in this data set?

```{r}

#Number of distinct titles

n_titles <- n_distinct(NETFLIX_DATA$title)
```

There are `r comma(n_titles)` shows and movies covered in this data.

###### 3. How many total hours have been spent watching shows from the Bridgerton universe?

```{r}
bridgerton_hours <- NETFLIX_DATA |>
  filter(str_detect(title, "Bridgerton")) |>
  summarize(total = sum(hours_viewed)) |>
  pull(total)
```

There have been `r comma(bridgerton_hours)` hours watched of Bridgerton universe during the date range described in the answer above for question number 1. 

###### 4. How many total hours have been spent watching the five seasons of Stranger Things? For this question, we only want the “real” Stranger Things shows and not the companion behind-the-scenes show (“Beyond Stranger Things”), the animated spin-off (“Tales from ’85”), or the background music (“Stranger Things: Fireplace”).

```{r}
stranger_hours <- NETFLIX_DATA |>
  filter(str_detect(title, "Stranger Things")) |>
  filter_out(str_detect(title, "Beyond Stranger Things")) |>
  filter_out(str_detect(title, "Tales")) |>
  filter_out(str_detect(title, "Stranger Things: Fireplace")) |>
  summarize(total = sum(hours_viewed)) |>
  pull(total)
```

The total amount of hours spent watching Stranger Things seasons 1 to 5 without including Beyond Stranger Things, Tales from ’85, and Stranger Things: Fireplace is `r comma(stranger_hours)`.

###### 5. What percentage of total watch time was spent on the Top 10 titles of 2026H1?

```{r}
#share of 2026H1 watch time captured by the Top 10 titles
h1_2026 <- NETFLIX_DATA |>
  filter(period == "2026H1")

# Total includes all viewing, including the "Other Shows" aggregate
total_2026 <- sum(h1_2026$hours_viewed)

# Rank real titles only: "Other Shows" is an aggregate, not a single title
top10_2026 <- h1_2026 |>
  filter_out(title == "Other Shows") |>
  slice_max(hours_viewed, n = 10) |>
  summarize(total = sum(hours_viewed)) |>
  pull(total)

top10_share <- top10_2026 / total_2026
```

The percentage of total watch time spent on the top 10 titles of 2026H1 was `r percent(top10_share, accuracy = 0.1)`.

###### 6. What fraction of Netflix’s catalog is globally available? (Answer this both by title and weighted by hours viewed)

```{r}
# Share of the catalog that is globally available

# By title: count each title once, then take the share that is global
global_by_title <- NETFLIX_DATA |>
  distinct(title, available_globally) |>
  summarize(share = mean(available_globally, na.rm = TRUE)) |>
  pull(share)

# Weighted by hours: share of all watch time that went to global titles
global_by_hours <- NETFLIX_DATA |>
  summarize(share = sum(hours_viewed[available_globally], na.rm = TRUE) /
                    sum(hours_viewed)) |>
  pull(share)
```

The fraction of Netflix's catalog available globally by title is `r percent(global_by_title, accuracy = 0.1)`. The fraction available globally weighted by hours viewed is `r percent(global_by_hours, accuracy = 0.1)`. This means less than a fourth are available globally and those same titles are the ones that have more than half of the watch time.

### Exploratory Questions (Table answers)

```{r}
library(gt)
```

###### 1. What was the top title (by total hours viewed) in each period and what fraction of total viewership did it capture?

```{r}
# Top title per period and its share of that period's total viewing.
# "Other Shows" is an aggregate bucket, so it is excluded from ranking
# but kept in the period total.
top_by_period <- NETFLIX_DATA |>
  group_by(period) |>
  mutate(period_total = sum(hours_viewed)) |>
  filter_out(title == "Other Shows") |>
  slice_max(hours_viewed, n = 1) |>
  ungroup() |>
  mutate(share = hours_viewed / period_total) |>
  select(period, title, hours_viewed, share)
# Average and highest share captured by each period's top title
avg_top_share <- mean(top_by_period$share)
max_top_share <- max(top_by_period$share)
top_by_period |>
  gt() |>
  tab_header(
    title = "Top Title in Each Reporting Period",
    subtitle = "Top shows but low Share of Period Viewing"
  ) |>
  cols_label(
    period = "Period",
    title = "Title",
    hours_viewed = "Hours Viewed",
    share = "Share of Period Viewing"
  ) |>
  fmt_number(hours_viewed, scale_by = 1e-6, decimals = 0, pattern = "{x}M") |>
  fmt_percent(share, decimals = 1) |>
  tab_source_note(md("Source: Netflix *What We Watched* reports, 2023H1–2026H1."))
```

We can see the top titles that appeared the most amount of times during the date period were "Squid Game Season 2" and "Bridgerton" (but 2 different seasons). It is surprising to see even the top titles only represent around `r percent(avg_top_share, accuracy = 0.1)` of Share of Period Viewing on average. The title that had the highest share of period viewing overall was "Wednesday: Season 2" in 2025H2 with `r percent(max_top_share, accuracy = 0.1)`. I also excluded "Other Shows" since it's not a title but a grouped total. 

###### 2. How has Netflix’s catalog changed in size over the periods for which we have questions? You should consider both the number of titles and the total runtime of content.

```{r}
# Catalog size per period: distinct titles, total known runtime (hours),
# and how many titles lack a runtime so the gap is visible.
catalog_size <- NETFLIX_DATA |>
  group_by(period) |>
  summarize(
    n_titles = n_distinct(title),
    total_runtime_hrs = sum(runtime, na.rm = TRUE) / 60,
    missing_runtime = sum(is.na(runtime))
  )
# Growth from 2023H2 (first comparable report) to 2026H1
start <- catalog_size |> filter(period == "2023H2")
end   <- catalog_size |> filter(period == "2026H1")

title_growth   <- end$n_titles / start$n_titles - 1
runtime_growth <- end$total_runtime_hrs / start$total_runtime_hrs - 1
catalog_size |>
  gt() |>
  tab_header(
    title = "Netflix Catalog Size by Period",
    subtitle = "trending up increase after 2023H1"
  ) |>
  cols_label(
    period = "Period",
    n_titles = "Titles",
    total_runtime_hrs = "Total Runtime (hours)",
    missing_runtime = "Titles Missing Runtime"
  ) |>
  fmt_number(c(n_titles, total_runtime_hrs, missing_runtime), decimals = 0) |>
  tab_source_note(md("Runtime totals include only titles with a published runtime."))
```

After reviewing the table above we can see that the period 2023H1 had the most amount of titles, the highest amount of Titles Missing Runtime, and at the same time the least amount of Total Runtime (hours), which can be attributed as to why the Total Runtime is so low compared to other periods. We can also see that from 2023H2 period on, both the Titles and Total Runtime (hours) started increasing slowly but steadily with the number of Titles growing by `r percent(title_growth, accuracy = 0.1)` and Total Runtime growing by `r percent(runtime_growth, accuracy = 0.1)` between 2023H2 and 2026H1. The Titles Missing Runtime for the rest of the Titles from the second period on are also very low so we can consider this data to be more dependable.


###### 3. Which titles have had the most consistently high viewership across all periods? These shows are likely to be ‘staples’ that viewers fall back on as ‘comfort food’, e.g., re-runs of Friends.

```{r}
# Staples: titles present in all 7 periods, ranked by their weakest
# period's hours (a high minimum means viewership never drops off).
# Standard deviation is shown to confirm how stable viewing is.
staples <- NETFLIX_DATA |>
  filter_out(title == "Other Shows") |>
  group_by(title) |>
  summarize(
    n_periods = n_distinct(period),
    min_hours = min(hours_viewed),
    avg_hours = mean(hours_viewed),
    sd_hours = sd(hours_viewed)
  ) |>
  filter(n_periods == 7) |>
  slice_max(min_hours, n = 10)
# Values referenced in the text
st4      <- staples |> filter(title == "Stranger Things 4")
escobar  <- staples |> filter(str_detect(title, "Pablo Escobar"))
heist    <- staples |> filter(str_detect(title, "Money Heist"))
staples |>
  select(-n_periods) |>
  gt() |>
  tab_header(
    title = "Netflix's Most Consistent 'Comfort Food' Titles",
    subtitle = "Users Go To"
  ) |>
  cols_label(
    title = "Title",
    min_hours = "Lowest Period (hours)",
    avg_hours = "Average per Period (hours)",
    sd_hours = "Std. Dev. (hours)"
  ) |>
  fmt_number(c(min_hours, avg_hours, sd_hours),
             scale_by = 1e-6, decimals = 1, pattern = "{x}M") |>
  tab_source_note(md("Titles appearing in all seven reports, 2023H1–2026H1."))
```

To create the table and define what is considered a "Comfort Food", I used the Titles that appeared in all 7 reports, and they are ranked by the lowest period to avoid the average being pushed up by temporary spikes. After checking the table above, we can see that both "Pablo Escobar, el patron del mal: Season 1" and "Chiquititas (2013)" have the highest Lowest Period since they are both over 105M hours. The highest overall Average per Period was "Stranger Things 4" by far with `r number(st4$avg_hours, scale = 1e-6, accuracy = 0.1, suffix = "M")` hours. This is a considerable difference compared to the other Titles, and the second Title with the highest overall Average per Period was "Pablo Escobar, el patron del mal: Season 1" with `r number(escobar$avg_hours, scale = 1e-6, accuracy = 0.1, suffix = "M")` hours. But this doesn't necessarily mean they are the top "comfort food shows" since we see other shows pop up multiple times just different seasons. For example: "Breaking Bad" Season 2, 3, and 5, meaning users came back to see a show that was released many years or seasons ago and still decide to spend their time watching it consistently over watching new shows. On the other hand, when we check how viewing behavior changes between periods (Standard Deviation(hours)), we can see the Title with the highest volatility is also "Stranger Things 4", which means even if it has the highest average within this top 10 Titles, it is not steady and it was just a big hit during a short period of time compared to the other shows. The Title with the lowest Standard Deviation (`r number(heist$sd_hours, scale = 1e-6, accuracy = 0.1, suffix = "M")`) was also the Title with the lowest Average per Period: "Money Heist: Part 1" with `r number(heist$avg_hours, scale = 1e-6, accuracy = 0.1, suffix = "M")` hours. This tells us even if it is at the bottom of the top 10 Titles, people watch it consistently and go to it as a trusted "Comfort Food Show".

###### 4. Within each period, what fraction of time was spent on ‘shows’ vs movies?

```{r}
# Heuristic: runtime over 240 minutes (4 hours) = TV show, otherwise movie.
# Titles with no runtime can't be classified and are shown separately.
shows_vs_movies <- NETFLIX_DATA |>
  mutate(type = case_when(
    is.na(runtime) ~ "Unclassified",
    runtime > 240 ~ "TV Show",
    TRUE ~ "Movie"
  )) |>
  group_by(period, type) |>
  summarize(hours = sum(hours_viewed), .groups = "drop_last") |>
  mutate(share = hours / sum(hours)) |>
  ungroup() |>
  select(-hours) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = type, values_from = share)

# Values referenced in the text.
# 2023H2 onward is used for averages because 2023H1 is missing most runtimes.
later <- shows_vs_movies |> filter(period != "2023H1")
first <- shows_vs_movies |> filter(period == "2023H1")

avg_tv_share    <- mean(later$`TV Show`)
avg_movie_share <- mean(later$Movie)
min_tv_share    <- min(later$`TV Show`)
max_tv_share    <- max(later$`TV Show`)

unclassified_2023h1 <- first$Unclassified
movie_2023h1        <- first$Movie

# Share of 2023H1 titles with no runtime (uses catalog_size from Q2)
missing_share_2023h1 <- with(catalog_size |> filter(period == "2023H1"),
                             missing_runtime / n_titles)

# Table
shows_vs_movies |>
  gt() |>
  tab_header(
    title = "Share of Viewing: TV Shows vs Movies",
    subtitle = "Shows win"
  ) |>
  cols_label(period = "Period") |>
  fmt_percent(-period, decimals = 1) |>
  tab_source_note(md("TV show = runtime over 4 hours; titles without a runtime are unclassified."))
```

To solve this question, I classified the titles as TV show if its runtime was over 4 hours, otherwise it is considered a movie. The titles that we have no runtime data of are considered "Unclassified" in order to check if there is a high number of Unclassified titles and make more accurate assumptions. This is a good way to organize the data because the runtime is available for most of the titles after 2023H1. 

I encountered a small limiting issue where short miniseries that are under 4 hours might be mixed in with the movies, and movies over 4 hours mixed in with shows, but this is very uncommon.

The analysis tells us that from 2023H2 on TV shows take between `r percent(min_tv_share, accuracy = 0.1)` and `r percent(max_tv_share, accuracy = 0.1)` of the hours viewed vs movies only `r percent(avg_movie_share, accuracy = 0.1)`. We can conclude this is stable since between years 2023 and 2026 there is not much fluctuation as seen in the table above. I am not using 2023H1 in this analysis since there is about `r percent(unclassified_2023h1, accuracy = 0.1)` of the share of viewing hours that is unclassified. But given the trend we could potentially assume since movies are still `r percent(movie_2023h1, accuracy = 0.1)`, about the same as the later average (`r percent(avg_movie_share, accuracy = 0.1)`), the unclassified data would be mostly shows.


###### 5. How does the performance of live events compare to pre-taped content? Does the average live event draw more viewership than an average piece of pre-taped content? How about a ‘top tier’ live event vs ‘top tier’ pre-taped content?

```{r}
# Compare average viewership overall and among each group's top 10%
# (top 10% is fairer than a fixed top-N since live events are rare).
live_vs_taped <- NETFLIX_DATA |>
  filter_out(title == "Other Shows") |>
  mutate(content_type = if_else(live_event, "Live Event", "Pre-taped")) |>
  group_by(content_type) |>
  summarize(
    n = n(),
    avg_hours = mean(hours_viewed),
    top10pct_avg = mean(hours_viewed[hours_viewed >= quantile(hours_viewed, 0.9)])
  )

# Values referenced in the text
live  <- live_vs_taped |> filter(content_type == "Live Event")
taped <- live_vs_taped |> filter(content_type == "Pre-taped")

gap_avg    <- taped$avg_hours / live$avg_hours          # how many times larger
gap_top    <- taped$top10pct_avg / live$top10pct_avg
live_share <- live$n / (live$n + taped$n)               # live events' share of rows

# Table
live_vs_taped |>
  gt() |>
  tab_header(
    title = "Live Events vs Pre-taped Content",
    subtitle = "Pre-Taped have the advantage"
  ) |>
  cols_label(
    content_type = "Content Type",
    n = "Titles (title-periods)",
    avg_hours = "Average Hours",
    top10pct_avg = "Top 10% Average Hours"
  ) |>
  fmt_number(n, decimals = 0) |>
  fmt_number(c(avg_hours, top10pct_avg),
             scale_by = 1e-6, decimals = 1, pattern = "{x}M")
```

When analyzing Live Events vs Pre-Taped Content, I compared the average hours per title, the overall, and the top 10% of each group. The top 10% is much more fair compared to a fixed top 10 because there are only `r comma(live$n)` live events vs `r comma(taped$n)` Pre-Taped.

I found Pre-Taped content wins Live Events in both categories: Average Hours by `r number(gap_avg, accuracy = 0.1, suffix = " times")` and top 10% average hours by `r number(gap_top, accuracy = 0.1, suffix = " times")`. This number difference gets bigger as you move from Average Hours to the top 10% Average Hours, meaning Pre-Taped has a lot more hours. It is important to point out there are very few Live Events, so this analysis is being based on that small sample. Also the hour length the events last makes a difference since short events are in the same category as multiple hour long events or seasons, so that makes Live Events look like they have a smaller viewer audience.

### Memo Supporting Calculations

```{r}
# ---- Trends over time (2023H2 = first comparable period) ----
# Global titles' share of viewing hours in each period
global_trend <- NETFLIX_DATA |>
  group_by(period) |>
  summarize(global_share = sum(hours_viewed[available_globally], na.rm = TRUE) /
                           sum(hours_viewed))

global_start <- global_trend |> filter(period == "2023H2") |> pull(global_share)
global_end   <- global_trend |> filter(period == "2026H1") |> pull(global_share)

# TV share of viewing, first comparable period vs latest
tv_start <- shows_vs_movies |> filter(period == "2023H2") |> pull(`TV Show`)
tv_end   <- shows_vs_movies |> filter(period == "2026H1") |> pull(`TV Show`)

# Share of viewing captured by the top title, first comparable vs latest
top_start <- top_by_period |> filter(period == "2023H2") |> pull(share)
top_end   <- top_by_period |> filter(period == "2026H1") |> pull(share)

# ---- Gini coefficient ----
# 0 = viewing spread evenly across titles; 1 = all viewing in a single title
gini <- function(y) {
  y <- sort(y)
  n <- length(y)
  2 * sum(seq_len(n) * y) / (n * sum(y)) - (n + 1) / n
}

# Formula check on a known example (expected result: about 0.555)
gini_check <- gini(c(20, 200, 0, 50, 40))

# Gini per period on raw hours and on views (length-adjusted).
# 2023H1 excluded: it lacks views and is formatted differently.
gini_by_period <- NETFLIX_DATA |>
  filter_out(title == "Other Shows") |>
  filter(period != "2023H1") |>
  group_by(period) |>
  summarize(
    gini_hours = gini(hours_viewed),
    gini_views = gini(views[!is.na(views)])
  )

gini_hours_latest <- gini_by_period |> filter(period == "2026H1") |> pull(gini_hours)
gini_views_latest <- gini_by_period |> filter(period == "2026H1") |> pull(gini_views)
```

### Corporate Strategy Memo

**To:** Netflix Leadership
**From:** Isabela Carvajal Rios
**Date:** October 16, 2026
**Subject:** [your title]

##### Summary
This memo analyzed Netflix's “What We Watched” reports, between the periods 2023–2026. The key takeaways are:
- Series took most of the watch time vs movies
- The global originals perform very well but the share of watch time is going down compared to the past
- The majority of the watch time comes from the broad title catalog and not the top hits.

In year 2027 Netflix should continue to grow and invest in their broad title catalog while keeping the originals and "Comfort Food" shows. They should also invest in TV shows like series or multi season franchises, and finally they should add more regional originals.

##### Global Originals
The global titles are a small part of the catalog representing only `r percent(global_by_title, accuracy = 0.1)` of titles. But at the same time they represent more than half of the watch time with `r percent(global_by_hours, accuracy = 0.1)` of viewing hours.

However, their share of watch time has dropped from `r percent(global_start, accuracy = 0.1)` in 2023H2 to `r percent(global_end, accuracy = 0.1)` in 2026H1.

This means while global titles are still going strong even if a fraction of the watch time fell, regionally available titles are taking a bigger share: `r percent(1 - global_start, accuracy = 0.1)` → `r percent(1 - global_end, accuracy = 0.1)`. To stay ahead, Netflix should keep investing in global originals while adding more regional ones.

##### TV Series vs Movies
The data shows that TV Shows are responsible for most of the watch time and it also grew slightly: `r percent(tv_start, accuracy = 0.1)` in 2023H2 to `r percent(tv_end, accuracy = 0.1)` in 2026H1. On the other hand movies are responsible for a small but steady share: `r percent(avg_movie_share, accuracy = 0.1)` on average. It is important to point out that every #1 title in every period was a series and not a movie.

Netflix should focus its budget for the coming year on series and multi season franchises vs movies since the data is clear that TV Shows are the ones being watched the most hours by the subscribers.

##### Big Hits vs the Long Tail
The Gini coefficient is a score that ranges between 0% and 100% to show how evenly something is divided (in this case, among titles). The closer the score is to 0% the more equally titles share the viewing, while 100% means one single title gets all the viewing.

Netflix's Gini shows subscribers' viewings are highly concentrated since it had a score of `r percent(gini_hours_latest, accuracy = 0.1)` in 2026H1 based on the hours viewed. And even after being adjusted for length to make sure it is fair between long shows and short shows, the Gini is still `r percent(gini_views_latest, accuracy = 0.1)` when measured by views. This has stayed very consistent since 2023H2 as can be seen in the chart below. 

Even though the viewing is concentrated, the data shows the top 10 titles take a very small fraction of watch time in 2026H1: `r percent(top10_share, accuracy = 0.1)`. So the majority of the watch time is spread among the rest of the title catalog.

This gives an important insight to Netflix that they need to keep a broad catalog of titles and not only rely on the top hits. 

##### Recommendations for 2027
- Prioritize series over movies, since we can see TV shows can account for `r percent(avg_tv_share, accuracy = 0.1)` of hours vs `r percent(avg_movie_share, accuracy = 0.1)` for movies.

- Keep the "Comfort Food" licenses and renew them since these shows are being continuously watched by the subscribers and have a steady engagement even if they came out many periods ago. A few examples are: "Breaking Bad" and "Suits".

- Continue investing in the creation of multi season franchises because the data tells us shows like "Bridgerton", "Wednesday", and "Squid Game" are #1 hits and there are returning viewers.

- Keep the broad range of titles and keep investing in having a full content library since the data shows the top 10 titles are only `r percent(top10_share, accuracy = 0.1)` of viewing, and most of the watch time is distributed among smaller titles. 

```{r}
# Visual: how concentrated viewing is, by period
gini_by_period |>
  pivot_longer(c(gini_hours, gini_views),
               names_to = "measure", values_to = "gini") |>
  mutate(measure = if_else(measure == "gini_hours",
                           "Hours viewed", "Views (length-adjusted)")) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = period, y = gini, color = measure, group = measure)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(size = 2.5) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent, limits = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(
    title = "Netflix Viewing Is Highly Concentrated",
    subtitle = "Gini steady at 75% since 2023H2",
    x = "Reporting period",
    y = "Gini coefficient",
    color = NULL,
    caption = "Source: Netflix What We Watched reports. 'Other Shows' excluded."
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```
